name: Tea bags on eyes

lead: Placing steeped, usually chilled tea bags over closed eyes is a long-standing home remedy for puffy or dark under-eyes. Proponents attribute the effect to caffeine and tannins, which they say tighten the skin and vessels around the eye, for a less puffy, brighter look.

Tea contains caffeine, polyphenols including tannins and catechins, and chemical analyses of commercial tea bags report considerable variability in these. Part of the effect may also come from the coolness and light pressure of the compress. No clinical study has examined tea bags on the eyelids.

paras: People steep two bags, let them cool or chill them in the fridge, then rest them on closed eyes for about 10 to 15 minutes, commonly in the morning.

The practice is generally described as low risk, though no safety data specific to it were found. Hot bags can scald the thin eyelid skin, and any plant product can cause contact irritation or allergy in some people.

chain: Caffeine and tannins act on skin
angle.text: Users lay steeped, chilled tea bags on closed eyelids to reduce puffiness and dark circles, citing caffeine as a vessel constrictor and tannins as astringent. It is common in beauty and looksmaxxing discussion; tea's chemistry has been analyzed, but tea bags as an eye compress have not been trialled.

lead: Tea bags on eyes is a home practice in which moistened or steeped tea bags, usually chilled, are laid on closed eyelids for several minutes to make tired, puffy or dark under-eyes look fresher. It uses an item already in most kitchens, which is much of its appeal in beauty and looksmaxxing discussion of the periorbital area.

Proponents attribute the effect to caffeine, which they describe as a vasoconstrictor that tightens dilated vessels, and to tannins, described as astringent. Tea does contain caffeine, polyphenols and catechins; chemical analyses of commercially available teas report wide variation in their phenol, catechin and caffeine content.[1][2] Wikipedia's dark-circle article likewise describes caffeine as a vasoconstrictor that can improve the look of dark circles and notes it is a common eye-cream ingredient.[3]

No clinical study has examined tea bags applied to the eyelids. Reference articles on periorbital dark circles discuss anatomical, pigmentary and vascular causes and list caffeine, vitamin C and other treatments, without naming tea bags.[3]
infobox: Steeped, cooled tea bags on closed eyelids

paras: The practice uses ordinary tea bags, most often black or green, which are steeped in hot water, cooled or refrigerated, and held against the closed eyes. Some accounts use herbal teas instead. Wikipedia's tea bag article describes the bag as a small porous pouch of tea leaves or herbs meant to be steeped in water.[4]

Proponents say caffeine narrows blood vessels and tannins tighten skin, reducing swelling and darkness. Laboratory analyses of tea have measured its total phenol, catechin and caffeine contents, which differ widely between products; caffeine in tea is reported at roughly 3 percent of dry weight.[1][2] Those analyses measure the infusion itself and do not address absorption through eyelid skin or any cosmetic effect.
The cool temperature of a chilled bag may contribute to a de-puffing effect independently of the tea; see the entry on cold compresses.

Wikipedia lists thin lower-eyelid skin, prominent underlying muscle, allergies and eye rubbing, medications, iron and B12 deficiency, sleep loss, age, sun exposure and excess melanin as contributors to dark circles.[3] A tea compress targets only the vascular and swelling component that proponents describe.

Research on sleep and looks reports that sleep-restricted people are rated as less attractive and less healthy, and measures periorbital darkness as one facial cue; sleep is therefore sometimes paired with eye compresses in routines.[5][6]

No safety data specific to tea bags on eyes were found. Generic concerns include burns from bags that are too hot, contact irritation or allergy to tea or its additives, and contamination of the eye area.
No studies found on tea bags as an eye compress. Related research is limited to chemical analysis of tea content and antioxidant capacity, which does not test appearance outcomes.[1]
